clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive group of storage disorders; types A and B result from deficiency of the enzyme acid sphingomyelinase, while type C is a distinct defect of intracellular cholesterol trafficking
Type A is a severe infantile neurovisceral form with hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, and rapid neurodegeneration, often fatal in early childhood
Type B is a chronic, largely non-neurological visceral form with organomegaly and pulmonary involvement that is compatible with survival into adulthood
A cherry-red macular spot may be seen, particularly in the acute infantile (type A) form
Type C arises from defects in the NPC1 or NPC2 proteins, causing impaired cholesterol handling and a variable neurological course
Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is a characteristic clinical clue to type C disease
Lipid-laden foamy macrophages (Niemann-Pick cells) infiltrate the marrow, spleen, and liver

Enzyme replacement therapy is available for the non-neurological manifestations of acid sphingomyelinase deficiency, and substrate reduction therapy is used to modify neurological progression in type C
reference.pathophysiology: In Niemann-Pick types A and B, pathogenic variants in SMPD1 reduce acid sphingomyelinase activity, so sphingomyelin cannot be hydrolysed and accumulates within lysosomes of macrophages and other cells, producing visceral organomegaly and, when severe, progressive neurodegeneration. Niemann-Pick type C is mechanistically distinct: variants in NPC1 or NPC2 disrupt the intracellular transport of unesterified cholesterol and other lipids out of the late endosomal/lysosomal compartment, leading to lipid accumulation, neuronal dysfunction, and secondary sphingomyelin storage. All forms are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Other lysosomal storage disorders with hepatosplenomegaly
Other causes of neurodegeneration with visceromegaly in infancy
additionalInvestigations: Acid sphingomyelinase enzyme activity in leukocytes for types A and B
Molecular genetic testing of SMPD1, or NPC1/NPC2 for type C
Bone marrow examination showing foamy storage cells when performed
Specialised biomarkers and cell-based cholesterol studies for type C
Ophthalmological examination for cherry-red spot and imaging for organomegaly and lung disease
redFlags: Rapid neurodevelopmental regression in an infant with hepatosplenomegaly
Progressive respiratory compromise from pulmonary infiltration in type B
New vertical gaze palsy or ataxia suggesting type C
Severe hypersplenism with cytopenias or risk of splenic rupture
reference.prognosis: Type A is uniformly severe with death typically in early childhood. Type B has a more favourable course with survival into adulthood, though pulmonary and hepatic disease may limit outcomes. Type C is progressive and variable, with age of onset strongly influencing survival; disease-modifying and supportive therapies can slow but not cure neurological decline.
pitfalls: Confusing the acid sphingomyelinase forms with type C, which requires different diagnostic tests and therapies
Attributing organomegaly solely to a haematological cause and missing a storage disorder
Overlooking vertical supranuclear gaze palsy as a specific pointer to type C
Assuming enzyme replacement will address the neurological features
management: Offer enzyme replacement therapy with olipudase alfa to address the non-neurological visceral and pulmonary manifestations of acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (types A and B)
For type C, use substrate-reduction therapy with miglustat to slow neurological progression, as this form is not correctable by enzyme replacement
Provide supportive care for organomegaly and hypersplenism, respiratory support for interstitial lung disease, and nutritional support for failure to thrive
Manage complications including bleeding from thrombocytopenia and intercurrent infection
Undertake surveillance of pulmonary function, liver and spleen, growth and neurological status appropriate to the subtype
Coordinate multidisciplinary care through metabolic medicine with neurology, respiratory and hepatology input, and offer palliative care in severe infantile type A
Provide genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
